\providecommand{\ptFindings}{}\renewcommand{\ptFindings}{With 200 test utterances, the mel distance was 0.665 with Phase~1 BiLSTM durations, 0.678 with phone-mean durations, 0.686 with global-mean durations and 0.666 with the acoustic model's own duration head; ground-truth durations gave 0.662. The paired bootstrap shows that BiLSTM durations are closer to the reference than phone-mean durations (difference $-$0.0136, 95\% CI [$-$0.0155, $-$0.0116]; closer on 89.5\% of utterances) and closer to the reference than global-mean durations (difference $-$0.0213, CI [$-$0.0243, $-$0.0185]). Against the model's own duration head the BiLSTM is practically equivalent to it (difference $-$0.0015, CI [$-$0.0023, $-$0.0005]; closer on 57.0\% of utterances). The BiLSTM closes about 82\% of the gap between the phone-mean baseline and ground-truth durations. Total-length error falls from 48.5 frames (phone mean) to 20.1 frames (BiLSTM). The absolute effect is small (2.0\% of the phone-mean distance): most of the remaining distance is already present with ground-truth durations and is due to the acoustic model, not to timing.}
\providecommand{\ptShort}{}\renewcommand{\ptShort}{the Phase~1 BiLSTM durations were closer to the reference than phone-mean durations in mel distance ($-$0.0136, 95\% CI [$-$0.0155, $-$0.0116]), while the effect size stayed small (2.0\%)}
\providecommand{\listeningParagraph}{}\renewcommand{\listeningParagraph}{A blind listening test (10 test utterances $\times$ 4 conditions) was prepared (notebook~14), but its ratings are not reported here because they did not meet our quality checks; subjective evaluation therefore remains future work, and the conclusions of this section rest on the objective measures above.}
